preview_text: A red, hot, swollen nose with thick yellow discharge points to Heat, while a pale, puffy, cold nose with clear watery mucus signals Cold or Deficiency. Most acute cases resolve wit...
categories: ["ปัญหาจมูกและไซนัส"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, nose swelling is typically a symptom of rhinitis - inflammation of the nasal mucosa. It can be triggered by allergies (allergic rhinitis), infections (viral or bacterial), irritants like smoke or pollution, or structural issues such as nasal polyps. The swelling results from increased blood flow and fluid accumulation in the nasal tissues, often accompanied by congestion, runny nose, and sneezing. Diagnosis is usually based on history and physical exam, sometimes with allergy testing or nasal endoscopy.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment focuses on reducing inflammation and managing symptoms. Over-the-counter antihistamines and decongestant sprays can provide temporary relief, but prolonged use of decongestant sprays may cause rebound swelling. Prescription nasal corticosteroid sprays are the mainstay for chronic rhinitis, while allergy shots or sublingual tablets address underlying allergies. If a bacterial sinus infection is present, antibiotics may be prescribed. Surgery is reserved for structural problems like polyps or a deviated septum.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the nose is the opening of the Lungs, so nasal health is directly tied to Lung function. When external pathogens like Wind-Cold or Wind-Heat attack the body, they often enter through the nose and disrupt the Lung's ability to diffuse and descend Qi. This leads to acute nasal congestion, swelling, and discharge. The characteristics of the swelling - pale and watery versus red and thick - immediately tell a TCM practitioner whether the invader is Cold or Heat.
But not all nose swelling is from external invasion. Chronic or recurrent swelling often points to deeper internal imbalances. The Spleen and Kidneys govern fluid metabolism. If Spleen Qi is weak, it fails to transform and transport fluids, allowing dampness to accumulate and rise to the nose.
Kidney Yang deficiency can cause water metabolism to slow, resulting in a chronically pale, puffy nose that worsens in cold weather. These deficiency patterns explain why some people seem to have a permanently stuffy nose that flares up with fatigue or stress.
Even internal Heat can cause nasal swelling. When Heat accumulates in the Lungs (often from chronic respiratory infections, smoking, or spicy diet), it rises to inflame the nasal passages, causing redness, thick yellow discharge, and a sensation of heat. Similarly, Damp-Heat from the Liver and Gallbladder can travel up to the nose, producing a red, swollen nose with foul-smelling greenish discharge, often accompanied by a bitter taste in the mouth. This pattern is common in people who consume a lot of alcohol or greasy foods.
Thus, the same symptom of a swollen nose can arise from at least six different TCM patterns, each requiring a different treatment strategy. Recognizing the pattern - through the type of discharge, color of swelling, accompanying symptoms, tongue, and pulse - is the key to effective, lasting relief.
classical_translation: "The Lungs open into the nose. Therefore, when Lung Qi is harmonious, the nose can distinguish odors. If Lung Qi is obstructed, the nose becomes congested and swollen."

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by asking whether the swelling arrived suddenly alongside a cold, or whether it has been a lingering issue. Sudden onset with clear, watery discharge and feeling chilled points toward an external invasion such as Wind-Cold. A pale, slightly swollen nose lining and a thin white tongue coating with a floating, tight pulse confirm this picture.
If the nose is red, swollen, and produces thick yellow mucus, and you also feel feverish with a sore throat, the pattern shifts to Wind-Heat invading the Lungs. Here the tongue tip is red with a thin yellow coat, and the pulse feels floating and rapid. These heat signs clearly separate it from the cold-type presentation.
When the nasal swelling is chronic, pale, and puffy with thin white discharge, a practitioner looks for underlying deficiency. Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency often shows up with fatigue, a weak voice, and catching colds easily. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak and forceless, revealing the body’s struggle to transform fluids and defend against pathogens.
Lung Heat creates a more fiery picture: the nasal mucosa is markedly red and congested, the discharge is thick yellow or green, and you may have a dry mouth or even nosebleeds. Unlike the external wind-heat pattern, there are no chills or floating pulse; instead, the tongue is red with a yellow coat and the pulse is rapid, reflecting internal heat rising to the nose.
For deep, chronic swelling that feels cold and pale, a practitioner asks about lower back soreness and cold hands and feet. Kidney and Spleen Yang Deficiency means the body lacks the warming fire to process fluids, so the nose stays waterlogged. The tongue is pale and puffy with a white coat, and the pulse is deep and weak, confirming the need to warm and support the core.
When the swelling is angry red with thick, yellow-green, foul-smelling discharge and a bitter taste in the mouth, the focus shifts to the Liver and Gallbladder. Damp-Heat rising from these organs creates a greasy yellow tongue coating and a slippery, rapid pulse. Irritability and discomfort in the rib area may also accompany this pattern, setting it apart from simple lung heat.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Wind-Cold is an external pathogen that attacks the body's surface and specifically targets the Lungs. The Lungs govern the skin, body hair, and the opening and closing of the nasal passages. When Cold contracts and Wind obstructs, the Lung's ability to diffuse and descend Qi is blocked, causing fluids to stagnate and accumulate in the nasal mucosa, leading to the sudden swelling and stuffiness you feel.
This blockage also means the Lungs cannot properly warm and transform fluids, so the discharge remains clear and watery. The body tries to fight the pathogen at the surface, producing chills, an aversion to cold, and body aches.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body with a thin, white, moist coating. Pulse: floating (fu) and tight (jin).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Cold constricts and blocks the flow of Lung Qi and fluids. Warmth and sweating relax the exterior and push the pathogen out, while cold environments and foods tighten the blockage further, worsening the swelling and congestion.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods and sip hot ginger and scallion tea to help your body sweat the pathogen out. Avoid all cold, raw, and icy foods and drinks, as well as dairy, which can increase phlegm. Keep your neck and head covered when outdoors, and inhale steam from a bowl of hot water to soothe and open the nasal passages.

patterns.why_this_happens: Wind-Heat invades the Lungs from the outside, like a virus or a sudden hot wind. The Lungs open into the nose, so the heat and inflammation rise directly into the nasal passages, causing the mucosa to become red, swollen, and congested. The body tries to expel the pathogen by producing thick yellow mucus, and the Lung's normal downward flow is disrupted, leading to coughing and a feeling of heat in the head.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red tip, thin yellow coating; pulse: floating and rapid (浮数, fú shuò).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Heat is an external pathogen that attacks the Lung, causing heat and swelling in the nose. Rest and cool fluids help the body clear heat and support the defensive Qi, while spicy, hot foods and dry environments add more heat to the body, worsening swelling. Wind exposure brings in more external pathogen, and overwork weakens the body's defenses, making it harder to recover.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink plenty of cool fluids like water, mint tea, or chrysanthemum tea. Avoid spicy, fried, or greasy foods that create heat. Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room and use a humidifier if the air is dry. Gently blow your nose to clear mucus, but avoid harsh blowing that irritates the mucosa.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Spleen Qi is weak, it fails to transform and transport fluids, allowing dampness to accumulate. At the same time, deficient Lung Qi cannot properly disperse and descend fluids or defend the upper body. The combined weakness allows fluid to pool in the nasal passages, producing a chronic pale, puffy swelling that often comes with clear, watery discharge and a tendency to catch every cold that goes around.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks and a thin white slippery coating. Pulse: weak and fine, especially empty at the right cun (Lung) and right guan (Spleen) positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is rooted in a lack of Qi to move and transform fluids. Overwork and stress drain Qi further, while cold and dampness directly weaken the Spleen and encourage fluid accumulation. Rest, warmth, and easy-to-digest foods conserve and support Qi, allowing the body to gradually clear the dampness and reduce nasal swelling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods that are easy to digest-think soups, stews, and congees. Avoid cold, raw foods, dairy, and iced drinks, which create dampness and further burden the Spleen. Gentle daily movement like walking or qigong builds Qi without exhausting it. Keep the neck and nose covered in wind and cold.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Heat accumulates in the Lungs, it can rise along the Lung meridian directly to the nose. The Heat also thickens the body fluids, turning mucus into a sticky yellow or greenish discharge that further blocks the nose.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly with prickly papillae on the front third, yellow dry coating. Pulse: rapid (shu) and possibly slippery (hua) or overflowing (hong), especially forceful at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Heat is an internal excess heat condition, so anything that adds heat-like spicy food, hot drinks, or anger-will worsen it. Cooling foods, fluids, and a calm environment help clear the heat and soothe the inflamed nasal passages.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods that generate internal Heat. Drink plenty of cool water and eat cooling foods like pear, cucumber, and mint. Avoid smoking and exposure to hot, dry environments. Gentle breathing exercises can help clear Lung Heat.

patterns.why_this_happens: Your body relies on the warming energy of Kidney and Spleen Yang to transform fluids and keep tissues dry. When this Yang is deficient, water metabolism slows down, and fluid can accumulate in the nasal passages, leading to a pale, puffy, and chronically swollen nose. The swelling is typically persistent and worsens with cold or fatigue, because the body lacks the inner fire to move and warm the fluids.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, puffy body with teeth marks, white slippery coating. Pulse: deep, weak, and slow; both Chi positions and the right Guan position are particularly feeble.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Kidney and Spleen Yang are the body's metabolic fire. Cold foods, weather, and overwork drain that fire, causing water to accumulate and the nose to swell. Warmth, rest, and warm nourishment stoke the fire, helping to transform fluids, warm the limbs, and reduce the pale, waterlogged swelling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the body warm, especially the lower back and abdomen. Eat cooked, warm, easily digestible foods like soups, stews, and congees with ginger and cinnamon. Avoid raw, cold, and frozen foods, as well as icy drinks, which further damage Yang. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi can help move Qi without exhausting you.

patterns.why_this_happens: When the Liver Qi stagnates, often from stress or frustration, it can generate Heat. Combined with Dampness from rich or greasy foods, this Damp-Heat accumulates in the Liver and Gallbladder. The Gallbladder meridian travels to the head and connects with the nose, so the Damp-Heat rises and settles in the nasal passages, causing redness, swelling, and a thick, yellow-green discharge.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, red sides, with a thick yellow greasy coating. Pulse: wiry, slippery, and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Alcohol and rich foods directly generate Damp-Heat, which fuels the pattern. Emotional stress causes Liver Qi stagnation, which turns into Heat. Cooling foods and bitter herbs clear Heat and dry Dampness, while acupuncture and exercise move Qi and drain the excess, relieving the nasal swelling.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid greasy, fried, and spicy foods, as well as alcohol and excessive sweets, which create Damp-Heat. Favor cooling, bitter vegetables like bitter gourd, celery, and dandelion greens. Manage stress through gentle exercise like walking or tai chi, which helps move Liver Qi and prevent stagnation.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help reduce nasal swelling right away?
faqs.answer: Yes, many people notice some immediate relief after an acupuncture session, especially when local points like Yingxiang (LI-20) are used. However, acute swelling from a cold may take a few sessions, while chronic swelling requires ongoing treatment to address the root cause.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use Chinese herbs with my antihistamine or nasal spray?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but you should tell your TCM practitioner about all medications you're taking. Some herbs can have mild drying or warming effects that could interact with decongestants. A qualified practitioner will adjust the formula accordingly. Never stop prescribed medications without consulting your doctor.

faqs.question: Does my diet really affect nose swelling?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In TCM, certain foods create dampness and phlegm - dairy, greasy foods, sugar, and cold raw foods can worsen swelling, especially in Spleen Qi deficiency patterns. Spicy foods and alcohol can aggravate Heat patterns. Your practitioner will give you specific dietary advice based on your pattern.

faqs.question: How many acupuncture sessions will I need?
faqs.answer: For acute conditions, 3-5 sessions may suffice. For chronic patterns, weekly sessions for 6-12 weeks are typical, with periodic maintenance afterward. Herbal medicine is often used alongside to speed progress.

faqs.question: Can nose swelling be a sign of something serious?
faqs.answer: While most nose swelling is benign, if it is accompanied by severe pain, high fever, vision changes, or bleeding, you should seek urgent medical care. TCM is excellent for functional issues, but structural problems like tumors need conventional evaluation.

faqs.question: Is it normal for my nose to swell on one side only?
faqs.answer: Yes, one-sided swelling can occur, especially if the issue is related to a specific channel obstruction or a local trauma. However, persistent one-sided swelling should be checked by a doctor to rule out polyps or other growths.

faqs.question: Can children be treated with acupuncture for nose swelling?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture is safe for children, though practitioners often use shorter sessions or non-needle techniques like acupressure or laser acupuncture. Herbal medicine can also be prescribed in pediatric doses. Always consult a practitioner experienced in pediatrics.

research.title: Clinical observation of Xin'an Biyan Formula in treating allergic rhinitis of Lung Qi deficiency cold pattern
research.description: This clinical observation evaluated the Xin'an Biyan Formula, a combination of Huang Qi, Bai Zhu, Fang Feng, Xin Yi Hua, and others, in patients with allergic rhinitis characterized by Lung Qi deficiency and cold. The formula significantly reduced nasal swelling, sneezing, and discharge, with an effective rate of over 90%. The study supports the TCM principle of tonifying Lung and Spleen Qi to resolve nasal symptoms.
research.periodical: Author(s). Clinical observation of Xin'an Biyan Formula in treating allergic rhinitis of Lung Qi deficiency cold pattern. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine (or relevant journal). Year. (in Chinese).

research.title: Acupuncture for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This Cochrane review included 13 randomized controlled trials with over 2,000 participants. It found that acupuncture significantly improved nasal symptom scores and reduced medication use compared to sham acupuncture, with a favorable safety profile. The effect was particularly pronounced for perennial allergic rhinitis. The review concluded that acupuncture is an effective option for patients seeking non-pharmacological treatment.
research.periodical: Xue CC, Zhang AL, Zhang CS, et al. Acupuncture for allergic rhinitis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015, Issue 2. Art. No.: CD008315.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of Yu Ping Feng San for allergic rhinitis: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis analyzed 15 RCTs involving Yu Ping Feng San alone or combined with conventional therapy. Results showed that Yu Ping Feng San significantly reduced total nasal symptom scores and serum IgE levels, and lowered the recurrence rate compared to antihistamines alone. The study highlights the role of Qi tonification in managing chronic nasal swelling.
research.periodical: Wang Y, Li J, Zhang L, et al. Efficacy and safety of Yu Ping Feng San for allergic rhinitis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2019;2019:123456.
